title: Efficient formation and identification of single emitters in 4H-SiC following maskless heavy ion implantation
authors: S. Eserin, L. K. S. Zimmermann, E. Schneider, M. Ludlow, J. Heiler, O. G. Lloyd-Willard, K. Stockbridge, G. Aresta, L. Antwis, S. K. Clowes, M. Hofmann, S. Kucera, P. Berwian, F. Kaiser, B. N. Murdin
abstract: Single photon emitters in silicon carbide (SiC) are a leading platform for scalable quantum technologies. Recent interest has focused on oxygen-vacancy-related emitters, which show exceptionally high optical brightness and strong spin readout contrast. One barrier to scalable quantum devices based on these emitters is the challenge of maskless formation and rapid identification. Here, we demonstrate the formation of isolated bright single emitters in 4H-SiC, using low-energy maskless implantation of heavy ions bismuth and tin. Following annealing, up to 18% of implanted sites host a single emitter, with optimal yields achieved at annealing temperatures of 900-1000 degrees C. Occupancy statistics are modelled to estimate the implantation dose that maximises single-emitter yield. We introduce a tiered characterisation scheme, where a simple intensity threshold isolates single-emitter candidates, confirmed through photon correlation measurements, after which correlations between polarisation, saturation count rate and magnetic resonance frequency assign emitter type. It is shown that time-consuming low-temperature spectroscopy is not necessary to distinguish emitter types. Together, maskless heavy-ion implantation and selective screening offer an efficient route to forming and rapidly identifying near-surface single emitters for room-temperature quantum technologies such as quantum sensing.
summary: This research presents an efficient, scalable method to create and identify single photon emitters in 4H-SiC using maskless heavy-ion implantation. By combining implantation with a tiered characterization process—including photon correlation measurements and ODMR—the authors demonstrate high yields and rapid type identification at room temperature. This advances the feasibility of solid-state quantum technologies.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently forming and rapidly identifying high-quality single photon emitters in silicon carbide (SiC) for use in scalable quantum technologies.
main_result: The authors demonstrated that maskless heavy-ion implantation combined with a tiered characterization scheme allows for the formation and rapid identification of single emitters, achieving yields up to 18% at optimal annealing temperatures.
method: The methodology involves implanting heavy ions (Bi, Sn) into 4H-SiC, annealing the material, and then using a multi-step screening process involving PL mapping, photon correlation measurements ($g^{(2)}(	au)$), and ODMR spectroscopy.
model_or_system: The physical system is single photon emitters (e.g., oxygen-vacancy related centers) embedded in 4H-SiC. The formation process is modeled using Poisson statistics to estimate the optimal implantation dose required to maximize the single-emitter yield.
key_observables: Second-order autocorrelation function ($g^{(2)}(	au)$), Photoluminescence (PL) spectra, Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) frequencies, and saturation count rates ($I_{	ext{sat}}$).
important_parameters: Optimal annealing temperature ($900–1000^\circ	ext{C}$); Single-emitter yield ($\eta$) up to $18\%$; Characteristic ODMR frequencies for different emitter types.
main_assumptions: The identification relies on the assumption that the brightest emitters are above a fixed count rate threshold, and that the Poisson model accurately describes site occupancy.
figures_summary: Figures show PL maps confirming single emitter locations, and detailed spectra (PL and ODMR) comparing the signatures of different emitter types (PL5 vs PL6) and their saturation behavior.

why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck in solid-state quantum emitters by providing a scalable, non-destructive, and rapid identification protocol, which is crucial for building quantum circuits.
